title: How Luel contributor tasks work
summary: A quick guide to why Luel creates contributor tasks, what happens after submission, and how contributors help build the next generation of AI.
body_markdown:
Luel contributors complete audio, video, image and evaluation tasks for AI projects. Those tasks do not begin with the contributor. They begin with something an AI team needs to collect, measure or understand.


A speech team might need conversations in a particular dialect. A robotics team might need first-person video of people completing everyday activities. A model evaluation might need human judgements on whether an output is accurate or natural. Luel turns requirements like these into tasks that contributors can complete.


At Luel, our network of more than 900,000 contributors gives us a way to collect that data across languages, locations and real-world conditions that are often missing from existing datasets.


## A task starts with a data need


Before a task appears on Luel, there is a specification behind it. That defines what needs to be collected, who should complete it and what a usable submission should contain.


The requirements can vary considerably. A speech collection might need native speakers of a particular language recording on their phones. A video project might ask contributors to perform named activities from a particular camera position. An evaluation task might ask contributors to listen to several model outputs and compare them.


Those requirements determine the instructions contributors see. The aim is to turn a broad need for data into something clear enough for thousands of people to complete consistently.


## Completing a task


Contributors can then take part in tasks they are eligible for. Each task explains what needs to be submitted and any requirements that apply to the collection.


Following those instructions matters because the value of a contribution depends on the project it was collected for. A clear studio-style recording may be useful for one speech dataset, while another may deliberately need ordinary phone audio with the variation of a real conversation. The same applies to video, images and evaluations.


The goal is not to make every submission look or sound the same. It is to collect the kind of examples the project actually needs.


## What happens after a submission


Once a task is submitted, it goes through review. The exact checks depend on the collection, but they are designed to confirm that the submission follows the instructions and can be used for its intended purpose.


For audio, that might mean checking the language, speakers and recording quality. For video, it could mean confirming that the requested activity is visible and complete. An evaluation task may be checked for whether it was completed correctly and consistently.


A submission can therefore be rejected even if the upload itself worked. What matters is whether it meets the requirements of the task.


## What accepted contributions become


Accepted submissions can then be combined with contributions from other people to form a larger dataset.


Thousands of recordings might become a speech corpus covering different speakers and accents. Video from many contributors can show how the same activity varies across homes, devices and people. Depending on the project, the files may also be paired with transcripts, labels, timestamps or other metadata before they are used.


This is what turns individual tasks into something useful for an AI team. Instead of relying only on data that already exists online, a collection can be built around the language, behaviour or environment a model actually needs to understand.


## How payments fit into the process


Each task sets out what contributors are being asked to provide and the payment attached to it. Different projects can have different rates, eligibility requirements and limits.


Payment is tied to the requirements of the task and the review process. A submission has to meet the collection criteria before it can be treated as accepted work, which is why review sits between completing a task and the final result.


## Why contributor work matters


Many of the things AI systems need to learn are poorly represented in existing data. Regional speech, everyday environments, human behaviour and knowledge from particular communities may exist in the real world without existing in a dataset a model can use.


Contributor tasks give Luel a way to collect that information directly. One recording, video or evaluation may be a small contribution, but combined with thousands of others it can help build datasets that reflect more languages, environments and real-world behaviour.


If you want to take part, you can[become a Luel contributor](https://www.luel.ai/contribute) and browse available tasks.
